title: ALMA Submillimeter Imaging of Betelgeuse Reveals Persistent Northeastern Hotspot and Corrugated Atmosphere
author: Bill Dent et al. / ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)
key_claims: ALMA extended-configuration observations (7 mas resolution, 16 km baseline) resolve submillimeter 'surface' of Betelgeuse at ~2,300 K
Northeastern hotspot persists for ≥7.3 years (2015–2023), far exceeding predicted convective cell lifetimes (months to few years)
Stellar radius deviates ±6% from circular; corrugated edge and molecular atmosphere (SiO, CO) show significant changes between epochs
Detached gas clump at ~10 km/s may connect to 2019–2020 Great Dimming event; companion star Betelgeuse B orbital axis aligns with hotspot geometry
If 2008/2015/2023 bright structures are same phenomenon, persistence approaches two decades
methodology: ALMA Band 6/7 submillimeter interferometry in extended configuration (16 km baselines); 2015 and 2023 epoch comparison; molecular line imaging (SiO, CO); astrometric alignment to <2 mas
key_risk: Companion-causation hypothesis is speculative; two-epoch data insufficient to securely link detached clump to Great Dimming; long-term hotspot persistence across 2008/2015/2023 not yet rigorously established as same structure
next_experiment: Third-epoch ALMA observation (2026/2027) to confirm hotspot persistence and measure proper motion; VLTI/GRAVITY companion orbit refinement; 3D radiation-hydrodynamic simulations incorporating companion tides and magnetic fields
notes: Excellent observational astrophysics. The persistent hotspot challenges standard convection models — a classic case where dominant theoretical paradigm (pure convection) may need revision. Companion-induced tidal locking or polar convection preference are alternative hypotheses. Directly relevant to C9 stellar-evolution complexity metrics.
